contact_edits.before: That leaves the gods, who speak a prologue that's bland to them, but bitterly ironic for everyone else. Greek tragedy draws on a vast mythological corpus: The writers could light up parts of the canvas as they chose, confident that their audience could fill gaps and draw conclusions. It's not so much subtext as ubertext. Here we have Poseidon and Athena, miffed that the Greeks haven't been making them the proper sacrifices, capriciously plotting their downfall, which will happen after the play ends. Poseidon, god of the ocean, is in naval uniform, and the two of them appear to be hanging out on the gangway of some beached battleship. I find the Greek view of divinity, Euripides' anyway, very plausible. It's the only theology that answers that old question about bad things happening to good people. The gods have the power but, with all that immortality to play with, they long ago got bored with us. In another view, they are us magnified, mainly for the worse. The Trojan Women is maybe the prime example of a play that's great without being, in any conventional sense, good. It has no plot, only episodes. It ends with Troy in flames: the only possible climax but halfheartedly depicted here. If you want to know what burning Troy was really like then, in a Stratford season full of cross-references, stroll along the Avon and catch the First Player's speech in Hamlet. - The Trojan Women runs until Oct. 5.
